frozen: 2026-11-01, after the Pinhasi et al. 2005 site table was parsed (row counts, columns and coordinates only; no distance, date or cost was compared) and before any run below.
question: Layer 2 of the language areas from below: farming spreads from climate hearths. Does a farming wave that moves through terrain, sea crossings and the map's own crop rules predict when farming arrived better than plain distance?

data.sites: Pinhasi, Fort & Ammerman 2005, PLoS Biology 3(12): e410, Supporting Information 1 (data/cache/pinhasi2005/st001.xls): rows tagged SITE with a calibrated date (CAL C14 BP). Regions 'Near East', 'Anatolia', 'Europe' and 'Iberia' (727 sites); 'Arabia' (Arabian Bifacial Tradition herders) and 'Asia' (east of the Caspian) are left out, as the paper's analysis is the Near East and Europe.
data.origins: the paper's 37 candidate origins: the 25-point grid HOA1-25, its two reference points and the ten named early sites (Catalhoyuk to Ali Kosh, with Ammerman & Cavalli-Sforza's centre).
data.climate: WorldClim 2.1 monthly climate, 1970-2000, 5 arc-min, window 24-62 N, 12 W - 56 E. Present climate, not the early Holocene: a stated limit of the test.

suitability: s = max(kcal_wheat, kcal_barley) x arable share, from scripts/land_people.py's analyse() unchanged (the rules the fantasy map uses; rivers and relief as in scripts/land_people_earth.py), divided by its 95th percentile over the window's land and clipped to [0, 1]. Wheat and barley are the Near Eastern package; millet, rice and dates are not used.
grid: 0.25 deg cells (3 x 3 WorldClim cells, mean of s over land, land if half the cells are land); 8-neighbour graph, longitudes not wrapped.

models.M0: great-circle distance from the origin (the paper's G columns).
models.M1: the paper's own shortest-path distance (its non-G columns).
models.M2: terrain and sea: travel time on the graph, land edges by Tobler's hiking function on the cell-mean elevation, sea edges at kappa times the flat-land time per km. kappa fitted from {1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 10}.
models.M3: M2 with farming: each land edge's time is divided by max(s, 0.05)^beta averaged over its two ends (a Fisher wave's speed goes as the square root of the growth rate, so beta = 0.5 is the textbook value). kappa as M2, beta fitted from {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5}.

fit: For every model the date is a straight line in the model's distance, date = a - b x d, least squares over the training sites. The origin (one of the 37) and the model's parameters are chosen on the training sites by the smallest root-mean-square error.
test: Leave one block out over seven blocks, each predicted from a fit on the other six: (1) Near East and Anatolia, with Cyprus; (2) southeast Europe: Greece, Thrace and European Turkey, Macedonia, Bulgaria, Romania, Serbia and Yugoslavia, Croatia, Bosnia, Hungary; (3) Italy; (4) Iberia and France, with Andorra; (5) central Europe: Austria, Switzerland, Germany, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Lithuania, Belgium, Netherlands; (6) Britain and Ireland; (7) Denmark and Sweden. Score: root-mean-square error in years over all held-out sites; also each block's error and the held-out correlation.

adopt_if.M3: M3's held-out error is at most 0.95 x the smallest of M0, M1 and M2, and M3 beats M2 in at least 4 of the 7 blocks. Then layer 2 on the fantasy map spreads farming with M3's rule and fitted parameters.
adopt_if.M2: if M3 fails but M2 is at most 0.95 x min(M0, M1) and beats M0 in at least 4 blocks, layer 2 spreads farming through terrain and sea without the crop term.
adopt_if.else: layer 2 spreads farming by plain distance from its hearths; the crop rules then only decide where farming can take root (s >= 0.05), not how fast it gets there.

also_reported: the fitted speed in km per year (the paper found about 0.6-1.3), the best origin on all sites, and maps of each model's residuals, especially the delay into the north (Britain, Ireland, Scandinavia) that a crop term should explain if climate set the pace.
